topic: Design cases: chat, feed & ride tracking apps

questions.question: Two people in a chat send messages at almost the same moment. How should every client order the conversation?
options: By the order each client received the messages, since that is how the conversation happened from its view
By a sequence number the server assigns per conversation, with the user's own unacked messages shown as pending at the end
By message ID sorted as text, since UUIDs generated on the devices increase over time
By the sender's device timestamp, since that records when each person actually pressed the send button
questions.explanation: A server-assigned sequence gives every participant the same order, which device clocks (skew) and arrival order (network jitter) cannot. Pending local messages sit at the end until the ack gives them their real position. Random UUIDs (v4) are not ordered at all.

questions.question: In a ride-tracking map, the rider's app should animate or interpolate the driver's marker between location updates instead of jumping it each time an update arrives a few seconds apart.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Updates arrive every few seconds and with jitter, so drawing each raw point makes the car teleport. Interpolating along the path (often after the server snaps points to the road) with the bearing for rotation makes it look continuous. If an update is late, the client can keep extrapolating briefly, then correct smoothly.

questions.question: In a design for a personalised home feed, where should ranking happen and why?
options: Entirely on the client, so the server only returns raw posts and the device sorts them by its own signals
On the client for Android and on the server for iOS, since iOS background limits stop local computation
Mostly on the server, so ranking can change and be A/B tested without an app release; the client caches and renders the result
In the push service, which ranks posts before delivering them so the app never needs to request the feed
questions.explanation: Ranking depends on large models and global signals, and needs to change often, which a server can do instantly for every app version. The client still does light work such as removing already-seen items or reordering for local actions. Putting ranking only in the app ties every change to store releases and old versions.

questions.question: How should a driver app collect and send location during an active trip to balance accuracy and battery?
options: Have the server send a push every few seconds asking the driver app to report its current location
Read raw GPS every second all the time and send each fix in its own HTTPS POST so the server has every point
Use the fused provider / CLLocationManager with intervals tied to trip state, batch a few fixes, and send them over the open connection
Use only significant-location-change updates during the trip, since they are the most battery-efficient option
questions.explanation: Active trips need fixes every few seconds, but idle drivers do not, so intervals and accuracy should follow the trip state; batching and reusing one connection cuts radio wake-ups, which dominate battery cost. One POST per second keeps the radio on permanently. Significant-change updates are far too coarse for a live trip, and push-driven polling is unreliable and wasteful.

questions.question: Which choices fit the local data layer of a mobile chat app? Select all that apply.
options: Per-conversation sync from the last known sequence number on reconnect or app open
Downloading the full history of every conversation on each launch so search always has all the data
A local table indexed by (conversationId, sequence) so history pages quickly from disk
Storing images and videos as BLOB columns in the message table so a message and its media load together
An outbox of unsent messages retried with the same client-generated ID until acked
questions.explanation: Indexed local history, gap-based sync and an idempotent outbox are the core of an offline-capable chat client on both platforms. Large media belongs in files (with a path or URL in the row); big BLOBs bloat the database and slow every query and cursor window. Full re-downloads do not scale with long histories.

questions.question: How should typing indicators be delivered in a chat app?
options: By polling a REST endpoint every second while the conversation is open, to keep the logic simple
Sent as FCM / APNs notifications so that users who have the app closed can see who is typing
Stored in the local database and synced through the outbox so that no typing event is ever lost
As short-lived, best-effort events over the live connection with a short expiry, not stored and not sent as push
questions.explanation: Typing state is only useful for a few seconds, so losing one is harmless and storing or retrying it is waste. An expiry (e.g. hide after a few seconds without a refresh) handles dropped 'stopped typing' events. Pushing it would spam devices, and per-second polling burns battery and server capacity.

questions.question: Fan-out on write (precomputing each follower's feed when someone posts) is the best default for every account, because it keeps both posting and reading cheap whatever the follower count.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Fan-out on write makes reads cheap but posting expensive: a celebrity post must be written into millions of feeds. Large systems use a hybrid, fanning out for normal accounts and merging posts from very popular accounts at read time. As a mobile engineer you mainly need to know that this is why feed freshness can differ per author.

questions.question: A rider books a trip and then locks the phone. Product wants live ETA on the lock screen. Which approach is realistic?
options: Schedule BGAppRefreshTask / periodic WorkManager to poll the trip API every five seconds while it is locked
Ask the rider for background location and work out the ETA on the rider's own phone every few seconds
Keep the WebSocket open in the background on both platforms and redraw a notification from every socket message
iOS: a Live Activity updated with ActivityKit push updates. Android: an ongoing notification refreshed by server pushes
questions.explanation: Live Activities are designed for this and can be updated through APNs without the app running; on Android an ongoing notification updated from FCM messages works. Background sockets get suspended on iOS and are costly on Android. The rider's location is irrelevant to the driver's ETA, and neither scheduler runs anywhere near every five seconds.

questions.question: A group chat has 5,000 members. Per-message, per-user read receipts are overwhelming the backend and clients. What is the better design?
options: Keep per-message receipts and push every receipt to all 5,000 members, but batch them every ten seconds
Drop the server entirely for receipts and have members' devices send them peer-to-peer to each other
Keep per-message receipts but send them over FCM / APNs instead of the socket so the server does less work
Track one 'last read sequence' per user per conversation, and derive counts or 'seen by' lazily when someone asks
questions.explanation: Reading is monotonic, so a single watermark per user implies every earlier message is read: storage is O(members) instead of O(messages × members). 'Seen by' lists can be computed on demand for a single message. Changing the transport or batching keeps the same huge fan-out.

questions.question: Driver location in your ride app is noisy (jumps, tunnels, late uploads). Which measures improve the tracked route and its use? Select all that apply.
options: Snap points to the road network (map matching) on the server before drawing or using them
Draw straight lines between every raw point as it arrives, since that is the most accurate record of the trip
Compute the final fare on the driver's phone from its local GPS trace, then upload only the total
Send a timestamp and sequence number with each point so late or out-of-order batches are handled correctly
Drop or down-weight fixes with poor reported horizontal accuracy before sending or using them
questions.explanation: Map matching, accuracy filtering and ordering metadata are standard ways to turn noisy fixes into a usable route. Raw points include jumps across buildings and rivers. Fare must be computed on the server from validated data; a client-side total is easy to tamper with and cannot be audited.
